**Simple Baselines Tie with BERT: A Leakage-Aware Comparison of Word Representations and Model Families for Psychological Manipulation Type Classification**

**Rifat Bin Sadeque**

**Nishan Nasim Rudra**

**MD. Tahsin Ibn Hasan** 

**Ateaf Akram Chowdhury**

**Department of Computer Science and Engineering**

**CSE440: Natural Language Processing II — Lab Project**

**Abstract**

Seven types of English conversational data are defined based on psychological manipulation in this paper. In order to reduce any possibility of data leakage, the data is grouped using template clustering on the basis of character level TF-IDF similarity followed by **StratifiedGroupKFold** splitting. This experiment involves a total of four embedding techniques; Word2Vec and GloVe for ten model families consisting of classical learners, recurrent models, and BERT. Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, and BERT Base models have perfect correction of the test dataset with macro-F1 of 1.0000. Of these, the Logistic Regression, which performs as good as BERT but with significantly less computational expense and fast runtime, can be considered a better alternative. Ablation experiments show bidirectional models and task-specific embeddings greatly improve performance of sequence models. On the other hand, handmade problems result in an accuracy between 0.57 and 0.86. This shows the poor generalization ability of models on natural conversation even when trained on highly accurate synthetic benchmarks.

**1 Introduction**

The meaning of psychological manipulation is far more important than particular abusive words, and can be achieved through the use of phrasing, implication, conversations and context. The message if you really love me, you would… is an affection message, which is implied to be under pressure, which depends on the nature of the conversation and on the sender of the message. Labels are subjective (interpretative) – mistakes can have far-reaching consequences – any good academic experiment would differentiate between what is considered 'benchmark performance' and any diagnosis, judgement between people etc.  
A common pipeline is provided which can be used for testing simple lexical methods, simple recurrent methods, bidirectional models and transformer models. The dataset is Kaggle Psychological Manipulation Conversations Dataset (Abbas, n.d.), which consists of 10,000 synthetic conversations in English, where the latter are annotated with respect to their target 'manipulation\_type', which has 7 classes. This data set is of interest for the second methodological interest. Hundreds of identical user groups and thousands of duplicate or similar conversations as a template are found in each group of users. If a random split was done naively, this would yield a split where the same template could be used in each split, and thus have higher scores. Thus it is explicitly addressed in the approach, and treated along with the treatment of duplicate detection and leakage-aware splitting.  
The study has the following four research questions:  
RQ1. What are the behaviors of the sparse TF-IDF representations, train-only Word2Vec representations, pretrained GloVe and contextual BERT WordPiece representations on this data?  
RQ2. Which of the good classical models or the recurrent, bidirectional or transformer model is better?  
RQ3. How do the results of the validation change as a function of the pre-processing, embedding scheme for the source, the source input, directionality and splitting policy?  
RQ4. In the randomizing of the data will random numbers be selected from a small subset of the examples with the word not available?  
For each family we consider 30 different configurations (one per every family) and for each family select the configuration with the best accuracy on the validation set; then for all 10 models, we test them once on a frozen and group-disjoint test set to answer the above questions. Two sets of manual diagnostic ablations have been reported on as well as one soft voting ensemble, and detailed results for error analysis for validation only ablations.  
The results are: (i) Logistic Regression has the optimal architecture of 1.0000 macro-F1 when the accuracy is maximum, meaning that this does not benefit from increased complexity (ii) The result of its evaluation of the manually written examples is much weaker, suggesting that the maximum score is not the result of solving a task, but rather of a good recurring lexical cue in a synthetic distribution (iii) In the terms of storage efficiency, Logistic Regression is the most optimal model with 0.25 MB of storage, while BERT achieves 418.59 MB.

**2 Related Work**

The focus of previous natural language processing studies has mostly been on hate speech and toxicity, characterized by surface-level hints relatively easy to identify as pointed out by Waseem and Hovy (2016) and Davidson et al. (2017). Manipulation, on the other hand, is subtle and gradually happens through the conversation, and gaslighting implies denial of reality by the manipulator over time. The studies closest to the current assignment is MentalManip by Wang et al. (2024) offering 4,000 annotated fictional conversations for detailed analysis of the manipulation techniques and the vulnerability of victims, claiming that the task is difficult even for LLMs. The current dataset is rather large (10,000 conversations), single-labeled, artificial, covering seven manipulation types, and including the neutral one. Our hypothesis is that the heavily manipulated and synthetic nature of the dataset generates abnormal lexical regularity. Another frequent finding for classification tasks is the usefulness of a simple linear model with good parameters working on n-grams representation that is sparse but competes with more sophisticated architectures, such as neural networks. Simple Naive Bayes classifiers have proven their competitive performance against more powerful ones in sentiment and topic analysis as stated by Wang and Manning (2012). The TF–IDF is still a robust benchmark for the representation, as emphasized by Salton and Buckley (1988).  
The first approaches are Word2Vec of Mikolov et al. (2013) and its effective distributional word embeddings based on vector learning from global co-occurrences with negative sampling; and GloVe of Pennington et al. (2014) and its vectors based on global co-occurrence in large-scale corpora. The recurrent models considered act on static embeddings; we will compare here task-specific skip-gram model and task-specific model using 50 pre-trained embeddings.

Processing of long texts occurs in chunks consisting of sentences. In this case, recurrent networks use LSTM gating to learn long-range dependencies (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997\) and GRU with a less complex gating mechanism (Cho et al., 2014). Our controlled ablations directly measure the advantage of using bidirectional encoders, which can process sequences in both directions (Schuster & Paliwal, 1997). This feature is inherent in pre-transformer text classification approaches (Vaswani et al., 2017), and can be applied to efficiency comparison.

BERT (Devlin et al., 2019\) created a new standard for sentence- and document-level classification with fine-tuning. Sun et al. (2019) defined commonly accepted rules for the learning rate, batch size, and sequence length, which have been used later in the Hugging Face Transformers library (Wolf et al., 2020). As the classical machine-learning part, we use scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011), gensim (Řehůřek & Sojka, 2010), Keras (Chollet et al., 2015), TensorFlow (Abadi et al., 2015), and PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019).

In recent research, it was shown that repeated training samples have a negative effect on language model performance (Lee et al., 2022\) and that contamination of benchmark can lead to incremental improvement of performance metrics (Sainz et al., 2023). Based on these insights for a classification benchmark, the template investigation counts the doubled structure, which is exactly or almost exactly doubled in the split, and then uses group-constrained cross-validation. 

**3 Methodology**

A complete experiment is performed, wherein three controls are involved. The use of only the text and indicators of the speaker/utterance as the input to the predictive features is allowed; the rest of the 21 fields in the metadata are excluded. It is done by the program via an exclusion of the fields list. The second control involves performing all of the representations and model selection on the training and validation sets. Finally, the test set is kept frozen until the choice of the configuration of each family is done. Throughout the whole process, random number seed \= 42\.

**3.1 Dataset**

The Psychological Manipulation Conversation Dataset (Abbas, n.d.) consists of 10,000 records of synthetic conversational examples with manipulation labels and descriptive metadata, with the exception of the examples' length, which equals the number of fields. The Psychological Manipulation Conversation Dataset (Abbas, n.d.) contains 10,000 conversation examples, where each row corresponds to one example's length, as well as manipulational labels and descriptive metadata. All entries have an inner field "messages", which includes speaker, text and sentiment\_score. Only the "speaker" and "text" are stored, "sentiment\_score" is discarded. There are seven classes for the target or “manipulation\_type”. All of 10,000 conversations are successfully parsed. All identifiers are unique. All fields have no missing values.

**Class distribution:** It is a slightly unbalanced distribution. There are 1,600 records (16%) in the neutral class and 1,400 records (14%) in each manipulation class.

Like, affectionate terms for love bombing, terms indicating obligation and accusation for guilt-tripping, and denial terms for gaslighting. **3.2 Preprocessing**

Each dialogue is converted into an ordered sequence, which indicates who is speaking and when, including first turn \[TURN\] reply, but no identification of information. The four types of texts that give reason for minimal default are: manipulation is based on negation (e.g., “you never listen”), imperatives are punctuated, and speaker role is contrasted (e.g., “the teacher asked the students to work quietly”). These types of text are therefore not stemmed, not converted to lowercase, and have no stopwords in the primary representation. Sublinear weighting TF-IDF will help us to reduce noise of high-frequency words but keep them. The results of the ablation for validation demonstrate that this option has a negligible influence on the results of our signal; 1.0000 macro-F1 score was obtained for minimal and normalized texts using Logistic Regression probe.

**3.3 Duplicate Investigation and Group-Aware Splitting**

There is no duplicate record found by the full record duplication checker since the record is distinguished through the use of the identifier and metadata. Documents are represented by their TF-IDF, and brute-force cosine nearest neighbors (cosine similarity ≥ 0.98) are grouped together with exact duplicates using union-find, with TF-IDF coded using template texts and using a 3-5-gram window, a minimum document frequency of 2, and a maximum number of features of 30,000. The components created from these merges are groups used for splitting: 20-fold StratifiedGroupKFold (14 folds train, 3 validation, 3 test) ensures that each component is in exactly one fold and that about the same proportions are preserved. The integrity checks make sure that no record is duplicated, that there is no overlap between the records in the conversation-ID with respect to the conversation-ID range, and that there is no overlap between the records in the template-group with respect to the template-group range—these are simple to within 2 percent, and that the overlap between the   
conversation-IDs across the folds and the overlap between the template-groups across the folds is exactly zero.

**3.4 Word Representations**

All the Reps are fit using the training data only, with the split.   
**TF-IDF:** Word TF-IDF feature extraction, which is performed using only the training data, produces 2,859 features. Classical setups look into character TF-IDF as well, and Random Forest integrates TF-IDF with Truncated SVD. TF-IDF is especially applicable in cases where there are repeating lexical and short-phrase signals in labels.  
**Word2Vec:** Only during training time, a Word2Vec model (skip-gram) is trained from conversations. This model has a window size of five tokens, min\_count=2, negative sampling and 12 epochs. Word2Vec supports embedding for recurrent neural networks, as well as average embedding ablations.  
**GloVe:** The pretrained glove-wiki-gigaword-50 embeddings are a semantic comparison of 50 dimensions. They are general-purpose vocabulary from the large corpus, and thus can not be used for conversational synthetic cues.  
**BERT WordPiece:** bert-base-uncased provides contextual embeddings and a 30,522 vocabulary WordPiece tokenization. The seven-class sequence classification layer is fine-tuned with only training conversations, with validation checkpointing.

**3.5 Model Architecture**

Thirty configurations are evaluated: nine classical, eighteen recurrent/bidirectional, and three BERT.  
All 30 complete. Within each family, configurations are ranked by validation macro-F1, then validation accuracy; the winner is recorded before any test inference.  
**Recurrent networks:** The SimpleRNN, GRU, and LSTM architectures get a 70-token sequence input by the training-fitted Keras tokenizer along with embedding matrix generated using either Word2Vec or GloVe. The recurrent encoder is followed by a dropout layer and a seven-unit softmax layer.  
**Bidirectional networks:** Bidirectional SimpleRNN, GRU, and LSTM enclose the same base layers in a bidirectional encoder with respect to the same C1-C3 lattice, thus confining the influence of bidirectionality only. Chosen: BSRNN\_C3 (0.9937), BGRU\_C1 (0.9983), BLSTM\_C3 (1.0000). The impact of bidirectionality on the equivalent C1 architectures is to increase SimpleRNN validation macro-F1 from 0.5669 to 0.9714, GRU from  
**BERT Base:** **AutoModelForSequenceClassification** uses a 7-class classification head for the pre-trained model (109,487,623 trainable parameters). For training, the following settings are used with the   
HuggingFace Trainer: AdamW, linear learning rate with 10% warm up, FP16, determinism, epoch-level validation/checkpointing. All three BERT configurations reach 0.9995 validation macro-F1 at displayed precision; **BERT\_C1** is selected by the deterministic ranking.

| BERT\_C2 | 3e-5 | 8 | 2 | 0.01 | 3 | 0.15 | 128 | 0.9995 | 452.58 |

Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, and BERT Base **tie** at 1.0000 accuracy, macro-F1, and weighted-F1; no single model is the unique winner. All six neural sequence models exceed 0.969 macro-F1. Timing and size are measured on the Kaggle T4 reference runtime and should be read as recorded run data, not hardware-neutral benchmarks.

![][image4]

Figure 4: Official test accuracy/macro-F1 and efficiency (training time, inference time, serialized size) across the ten selected models.

**Best and worst configurations.** The optimal official result is a draw between the four models. However, for non-drawn models, LSTM and Bidirectional LSTM (0.9992 macro-F1) perform better than GRU and Bidirectional GRU. The worst performing model is SRNN\_C3 (0.9692) owing to its unidirectional vanilla recurrence which turns out to be the weakest encoder, matching up with C1 ablation (0.5669). SRNN\_C3 is also the slowest training neural network (74.7 s) due to the requirement of small batch sizes for the trainable-embedding version, while the fastest one is Bidirectional GRU (5.4 s). The most important comparison is made between Logistic Regression and BERT; despite equal official results, the former has 0.25 MB compared to the latter's 418.59 MB memory (a difference of ≈1,670), 1.48 s against 216.51 s training time, and 0.11 s vs. 2.30 s inference.

**4.2 Per-Class Results and Confusion Analysis**

The confusion matrices are presented in Figure 7 and the normalized confusion matrices in Figure 8.The per-class F1 and normalized confusion matrices are shown in Figure 7 and Figure 8, respectively. The tied models result in error-free diagonal matrices. The most common errors that SimpleRNN makes are displayed in Table 10 in the weakest model. These errors are semantically explainable, because they share affective words (charm/ﬂattery, love bombing/affection), surface politeness (passive aggression/neutral), and imperative pressure (guilt-tripping/coercion). SimpleRNN commits a total of 39 errors with mean conﬁdence 0.6260 on errors, wrongly classifies 11 manipulation examples as neutral, and makes no example as manipulation in the neutral subgroup (an undesirable asymmetry for a safety-related application), is least accurate on short conversations (0.9412 accuracy vs. 0.9742 medium vs. 0.9775 long), and is least accurate on the family context subgroup (0.9669).

Such errors are semantically explicable since flattery/charm and love-bombing involve affective lexicon and positive valence; passive-aggression and neutral share polite surface; guilt-tripping and coercion use imperative pressure. SimpleRNN makes 39 errors in total with average probability of 0.6260 to make such an error, predicts 11 cases of manipulation as neutral but does not predict any case of neutral as manipulation (which is a flaw in a potentially safety-sensitive task), performs worst at short conversations (0.9412 accuracy vs. 0.9742 medium, 0.9775 long) and in family subgroup (0.9669 accuracy).

Figure 7: Validation-only ablation results across the seven comparison families.

Two types of ablation exist. The effect of directionality provides the highest macro F1 variability (+0.40 for SimpleRNN), meaning that manipulation is influenced by both the past and future context. Source embedding adds to the performance of the Word2Vec model trained only for this task, providing a bonus of \+0.037. This can be explained through the consideration of the distant Wikipedia/Gigaword source of pre-trained GloVe embeddings. Speaker and preprocessing are equally important for this task, providing a result of 1.0000 in Logistic Regression probe. It should be noted that even the simple stratified split provides a result of 1.0000 in the same probe.

**4.4 Ensemble**

A representative for each group of complementary models such as the classical Random Forest, the recurrent Bidirectional LSTM, and the transformer BERT Base is chosen and used in a voting ensemble according to their performance on validation sets. The weights for the ensemble are found from a grid of weights whose values are 1-3 with uniform and normalized product values (final weights: 0.2, 0.6, 0.2) based on the probabilities obtained in validation. The soft voting ensemble has a test accuracy and macro-F1 score of 1.0000; but since the top-performing individual model has the same value of 1.0000, there is no improvement in macro-F1.

**Fourteen examples (two per class), Logistic Regression only:** 11 out of 14 (78.57%) correct. The 3 incorrect classifications are an example of gaslighting that was classified as being a passive-aggressive type, an example of guilt-tripping that was classified as direct coercion, and an example of passive-aggressive behavior that was predicted to be direct coercion.  
The official predictions have been more accurate than these ones (0.57-0.86 vs 0.97-1.00 accuracy). The example of passive-aggressive behaviour is especially difficult for all of the classification models as BERT classifies this phrase with a 9621 probability to be neutral, Logistic Regression and Naive Bayes classify this phrase as direct coercion. This implies that the synthetic examples are not a good representation of negated hostility. 

**5 Conclusion**

  This experiment used 10 models and 30 setups for the validation set, 10 setups for the frozen test set and 10 word embeddings, considering the leakage. Although advanced models outperform strong sparse baseline models in terms of official accuracy, they don't necessarily do so in terms of macro F1 scores: for the official accuracy, the scores are equal, at 1.0000, as is the case for the macro F1 scores. The clear lexical and n-gram features between the synthetic categories are explicitly learned by TF-IDF and can be used to compete with the 418.59 MB transformer, which is the reason why Logistic Regression is used as the benchmark model. Seeing that, the added complexity did not impact on performance (+0.00 macro-F1) but the impact was bi-directional (+0.40) in the embedding fit case (train-only Word2Vec vs pretrained GloVe) and unidirectional (+0.40) in the ablation case (architecture vs SimpleRNN). Due to 2,081 duplicated elements in the examples and 5,902 nearly duplicated elements connecting the partitions, it was necessary to use group-aware splitting. However, no matter how leak-proof the split is, it's difficult to get a templated synthetic benchmark to be a conversation\! The scores reflect the structure of data and not ability, as manual analysis (accuracy range: 0.57-0.86) versus perfection.  
**Future work:** Evaluation of independently collected data; Evaluation of data collected by multiple annotators, but with the data ethically managed; Evaluation of multiple annotators, human-created conversation; Evaluation of agreement score; Evaluation of multilabel versions; Robustness to paraphrase; Robustness to adversarial attacks; Robustness to counterfactuals; Robustness to time; Efficiency of compact contextual encoders; Efficiency of knowledge distillation with respect to Logistic Regression (human) evaluation; Human evaluation on preregistered, blinded challenge set; Evaluation on human review.

**Limitations**

Since the dialogues have been created from artificially created conversations through lexical templates, the process becomes easier as compared to the real-world scenario. Still, there can be some similarities in meaning between two different partitions despite the fact that the connected parts of templates cannot contain any meaning. The number of artificially created samples (seven and fourteen respectively) is small enough to make any statistical analysis on the population level. The results will be dependent on the dataset, restricted to the English language, specific to the label since some types of manipulations could be applied to different labels, runtime-specific to Kaggle T4.
